pests.name: Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
symptoms: small white insects flying up when plant is disturbed
yellowing and curling of leaves
sticky honeydew on leaves
black sooty mold growing on honeydew
stunted growth in young plants

favorable_conditions.notes: Populations build up fastest in warm, dry weather. Also a vector for Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus.

ipm_steps: Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce adult populations
Introduce natural predators such as ladybird beetles or parasitic wasps (Encarsia formosa) where available
Remove and destroy heavily infested lower leaves
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages tender growth favored by whiteflies
Use reflective mulches to deter whitefly landing
If chemical control is needed, consult local agricultural extension for approved insecticides and rotate modes of action to avoid resistance
sources: FAO Plant Production and Protection guidelines

pests.name: Aphids (various species)
symptoms: clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and undersides of leaves
curling or puckering of young leaves
sticky honeydew and sooty mold
stunted shoot growth
presence of ants tending aphid colonies

favorable_conditions.notes: Rapid reproduction in mild, dry conditions. Slowed by heavy rain and very high temperatures.

ipm_steps: Encourage natural predators (ladybird beetles, lacewings, hoverflies)
Use a strong water spray to dislodge small colonies
Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil for moderate infestations
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization
Monitor regularly during early vegetative stage when damage is most costly
sources: FAO Plant Production and Protection guidelines

diseases.name: Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
symptoms: dark brown spots with concentric rings (target-like pattern) on older, lower leaves first
yellowing of leaf tissue around spots
leaf drop starting from the bottom of the plant
dark sunken lesions on stems near the soil line
dark leathery spots near the stem end of fruit

favorable_conditions.notes: Favored by warm temperatures with alternating wet and dry periods, and by plant stress or nutrient deficiency.

ipm_steps: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves promptly
Improve air circulation through proper plant spacing and staking
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant
Apply mulch to reduce soil splash onto lower leaves
Practice crop rotation (avoid planting tomato/potato family in the same spot for 2-3 years)
Use approved protectant fungicides preventively in high-risk weather if recommended locally

diseases.name: Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans)
symptoms: large irregular water-soaked dark green to brown patches on leaves
white fuzzy fungal growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
rapid collapse and blackening of foliage
firm dark brown greasy-looking lesions on fruit
characteristic musty odor in severe infections

favorable_conditions.notes: Spreads explosively in cool, wet, humid weather with extended leaf wetness. Can destroy a crop within days under favorable conditions.

ipm_steps: Act quickly: this disease can spread and cause major losses within days
Remove and destroy (do not compost) infected plants immediately
Avoid overhead irrigation and reduce canopy humidity
Improve drainage and spacing for air circulation
Apply protectant or curative fungicides recommended by local extension services promptly in high-risk weather
Avoid planting near infected potato crops, as both share this pathogen

diseases.name: Septoria Leaf Spot (Septoria lycopersici)
symptoms: small circular spots with dark brown margins and gray/tan centers on lower leaves
tiny black specks (fungal fruiting bodies) visible in spot centers
progressive yellowing and leaf drop from the bottom up
spots generally do not affect fruit directly but defoliation reduces yield and sunscald risk

favorable_conditions.notes: Favored by extended leaf wetness from rain, dew, or overhead irrigation.

ipm_steps: Remove infected leaves and clean up plant debris after harvest
Avoid overhead watering; water at soil level
Rotate crops away from tomato/potato family for at least a year
Stake or cage plants for better airflow
Apply fungicide preventively in wet seasons if recommended locally

diseases.name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
symptoms: upward curling and cupping of leaves
marked yellowing of leaf margins
stunted, bushy plant growth
flower drop and drastically reduced fruit set
transmitted by whitefly, so whitefly presence is a strong contextual clue

favorable_conditions.notes: Risk tracks whitefly vector activity, which is highest in warm, dry conditions.

ipm_steps: Control whitefly populations, since they are the transmission vector
Remove and destroy infected plants to reduce virus reservoir
Use virus-resistant tomato varieties where available
Use insect-proof nets or reflective mulch in nurseries to protect young plants
Avoid planting new tomato crops next to older infected fields

disorders.name: Blossom End Rot (Physiological Disorder)
symptoms: dark sunken leathery patch at the blossom end of green or ripening fruit
water-soaked flat lesion at the bottom of the fruit opposite the stem
rotting or premature ripening with black leathery surface on tomato bottom
damage confined to fruit blossom end with healthy foliage and stems

favorable_conditions.notes: Abiotic physiological disorder caused by localized calcium deficiency during rapid fruit expansion, triggered primarily by irregular watering, moisture fluctuations, and root damage. Not caused by a pathogen or pest.

ipm_steps: Maintain consistent, even soil moisture through regular scheduled irrigation; avoid cycles of extreme drought followed by heavy flooding
Apply organic or plastic mulch around plants to conserve soil moisture and stabilize soil temperature
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer (especially ammonium-based), which drives excessive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit calcium uptake
Ensure adequate soil calcium and appropriate soil pH (6.2-6.8) prior to planting using agricultural lime or gypsum based on soil tests
Avoid deep cultivation or hoeing close to plant bases that could damage shallow feeder roots
Promptly remove affected fruits so the plant can direct nutrients to healthy developing fruit
